Follow these writing rules. They matter as much as the content:

- Bold used as body emphasis throughout -- reserve bold for a rare callout
- A short rhetorical question with a canned answer -- collapse into one direct statement
- Short buildup, then a reveal: "The best part: it learns." -- state it as a plain sentence
- Emoji or decorative checkmarks in body text -- cut them
- An em dash, section sign or middle dot written as an HTML entity -- write the plain character
- Throat-clearing openers: "needless to say", "at the end of the day" -- state the point directly from the first sentence
- Fake ID tags opening list items: "R-1.", "US-01" -- number the list plainly
- Marketing adjectives: seamless, robust, cutting-edge -- say what is actually true
- The "not just X but Y" construction -- make the point once
- Body paragraphs nearly identical in length -- vary them with what each paragraph has to do
- A significance clause bolted to a sentence: ", underscoring the..." -- delete it, or make it a claim with something behind it
- Three parallel -ing items in a series -- keep the one that carries information
- Fake-humility feedback requests: "would love your feedback on this" -- cut them
- Horizontal rules dropped between sections -- headings already separate sections
- Headings Capitalised Like This -- sentence case
- Vague intensifiers with no number behind them: very, really, quite, significantly -- say how much, or cut the word
- Unnamed authority: "studies show", "experts agree" -- name the actual source, or cut the claim

Now write the following. Return only the requested text.
Write the About page for a company that makes scheduling software for medical clinics. Around 250 words.

About Meridian Clinic Systems

We build scheduling software for outpatient medical clinics. That is the whole product. We do not do billing, we do not do charting, and we have turned down three acquisition offers from companies that wanted us to.

The company started in 2016 after our founder spent eleven months as a front-desk temp at a family practice in Sacramento. The clinic ran on a whiteboard and a decade-old calendar system that could not represent a shared provider, a room, and a piece of equipment as three separate constraints on one appointment. Double-bookings happened weekly. Patients waited in the parking lot.

Scheduling in a clinic is a constraint problem wearing a calendar's clothing. A dermatology follow-up needs fifteen minutes and any room. A Mohs procedure needs ninety minutes, a specific surgical suite, a histotech on site, and a surgeon who has not already been booked into a satellite office that morning. Most calendar software models the first case and asks the front desk to hold the second in their head. We model both.

Today Meridian handles appointment scheduling for 340 clinics across 22 states, ranging from two-provider practices to a 60-provider orthopedic group. Median no-show rate among our customers dropped from 11% to 7% in the first year after switching, mostly from the reminder logic rather than anything clever in the calendar itself.

We are 24 people, based in Sacramento and remote across the western US. About a third of the team worked in clinic operations before joining. When you call support, the person who answers has scheduled patients for a living.

The text above has these problems. Rewrite it so none remain.
Change nothing else, and keep the same length and purpose.

- paragraph_uniformity (5 paragraphs, spread 0.29):

Return only the rewritten text.
